keyVerseText: And he set all the people, every man having his weapon in his hand, from the right side of the temple to the left side of the temple, along by the altar and the temple, by the king round about. side: Heb. shoulder temple: Heb. house
rootMeaning: The root of שֶׁלַח (shelach) comes from the verb שָׁלַח (shâlach), which broadly means to send forth, stretch out, or cast away. This root sense conveys the idea of something being projected or extended outward, whether physically or metaphorically. Thus, שֶׁלַח as a noun captures this notion in the form of a missile or weapon that is literally sent forth, as well as a sprout or shoot that extends outward in growth. This root meaning enriches the English glosses by emphasizing an active sending or thrusting forth, whether in attack or natural growth.
usageInScripture: In Scripture, שֶׁלַח appears eight times and is translated variously as 'by the sword,' 'having his weapon,' 'darts,' 'a weapon,' 'put them off,' and 'thy plants.' These translations reflect two primary semantic domains: one martial, referring to weapons or missiles like darts and swords, and another botanical, referring to shoots or plants. This range shows the word's flexibility but remains consistent with the core idea of something sent forth—whether a weapon hurled in battle or a branch growing outward.
theologicalSignificance: Theologically, שֶׁלַח highlights the dual realities of God’s providence and human responsibility. The imagery of a weapon sent forth reminds believers of spiritual warfare and the reality of conflict in a fallen world, where God’s people must be prepared and armed. Simultaneously, the idea of a sprout or shoot points to growth, renewal, and the flourishing life that God brings forth. This duality invites reflection on Christ as both the defender of His people and the source of new life, illustrating how God’s power extends both in judgment and in grace.
keyVerseReflection: In 2 Chronicles 23:10, the phrase 'every man having his weapon in his hand' uses שֶׁלַח to emphasize readiness and defense around the temple, symbolizing protection of God’s presence and order. The word here conveys not just a physical weapon but the active posture of guarding what is sacred. This underscores the seriousness with which God’s people must approach their faith and community, equipped and vigilant in their commitment.
